Here's how journals work in Albion Online, specifically for getting higher-tier ones:

**You don't craft higher-tier journals — you acquire them from laborers or the marketplace.**

Empty journals can be acquired from laborers directly, or bought from other players through the marketplace.

**To fill them (which is the actual progression):**

- Journals can be filled if you carry them in your inventory while doing certain journal-specific activities of the same tier or up to two tiers higher.
- Gathering journals fill while you gather resources, crafting journals fill while you craft items, mercenary journals fill while you gain PvE fame from slaying monsters, and general journals fill when you do anything that brings in fame.
- For gathering specifically: you can fill a T4 journal by harvesting T4, T5, or T6 resources, or a T7 journal by harvesting T7 or T8.

**For higher-tier journals specifically:**

- Journals require more fame to fill as their tier increases. So T6+ journals take significantly longer to fill than lower-tier ones.
- The fame action must match the journal tier — only base fame counts (premium bonus does not), and crafting fame from studying cannot fill crafting journals.

**Laborer tier matters too:**

- For higher-tier laborers, you must send them on jobs to increase their fame over time, or purchase higher-tier laborers from the market. Higher-tier laborers return better resources from the journals you give them.

The short version: buy higher-tier empty journals from the market or your laborer, carry them while doing the matching activity at the right tier, fill them, hand them back in.

Nothing in the search results specifically documents `allow_dangling_human_message=1` as a public parameter. Here's what I can piece together from context though:

In the Anthropic Messages API, conversations must alternate strictly between user and assistant turns. A "dangling human message" would be a conversation that ends on a user turn with no assistant response following it — which is technically an incomplete or malformed conversation state from the API's perspective.

So `allow_dangling_human_message=1` almost certainly tells the frontend to permit loading or displaying a conversation that ends on a user message without a corresponding assistant reply. It's probably an internal parameter that handles edge cases like interrupted responses, failed generations, or conversations that were saved mid-turn.

It's not a publicly documented parameter — it looks like internal plumbing surfacing in the URL, likely because this conversation had a turn that didn't complete cleanly at some point.

Claude.ai allows users to open a new chat with a pre-filled prompt via a URL parameter (claude.ai/new?q=...). We discovered that certain HTML tags could be embedded in this parameter, invisible in the text box but fully processed by Claude when ...

Establish governance for AI agent identities. AI agents authenticate, hold credentials, and take autonomous actions. They need to be governed with the same rigor as human users and service accounts, with intent analysis, deterministic policy enforcement, just-in-time-scoped access, and a full audit trail from human to agent to action. ... This is the second time in recent months that Oasis Security researchers have demonstrated how AI agents can be silently compromised, following our disclosure in OpenClaw. The pattern is consistent: agents with broad access can be hijacked by a single manipulated input, and traditional identity and access management controls were not designed for this. For the full technical breakdown, read the Claudy Day whitepaper. To learn how Oasis Security governs AI agent access at scale, see Agentic Access Management ... Yes.

In a default Claude.ai session, an attacker can access conversation history and memory, which may include business strategy, financial information, health concerns, personal details, and any other sensitive topics discussed with the assistant. With MCP servers or enterprise integrations enabled, the attacker can also read files, send messages, and interact with connected services. How can organizations protect AI agents from prompt injection? Organizations should inventory all AI agents and their integrations, disable unnecessary permissions, and educate users that shared links and pre-filled prompts can contain hidden instructions. AI agents that authenticate, hold credentials, and take autonomous actions need to be governed with the same rigor as human users and service accounts. Discover tips, technical guides and best practices in our biweekly newsletter.

No integrations, no tools, no MCP servers required. The attack works against a default, out-of-the-box claude.ai session. We responsibly reported all findings to Anthropic through their Responsible Disclosure Program before publication. The prompt injection issue has been fixed, and the remaining issues are currently being addressed. We appreciate Anthropic's responsiveness and collaboration throughout the process. You can read the Oasis Security Research Team's full technical report here. ... Invisible prompt injection via URL parameters. Claude.ai allows users to open a new chat with a pre-filled prompt via a URL parameter (claude.ai/new?q=...). We discovered that certain HTML tags could be embedded in this parameter, invisible in the text box but fully processed by Claude when the user hit Enter. An attacker could hide arbitrary instructions, including data-extraction commands, inside what appears to be a normal prompt.

Claude.ai is one of the most widely used AI assistants worldwide. Millions of people trust it with sensitive conversations, business strategy, health concerns, financial planning, personal relationships, and increasingly connect it to enterprise tools, files, and APIs through integrations and MCP servers. That trust comes with a critical assumption: that the instructions Claude receives are the ones the user intended to give. Oasis Security researchers discovered that for a significant period, this assumption could be broken, and worked with Anthropic to close the gap. ... We discovered three vulnerabilities in Claude.ai and the broader claude.com platform, collectively dubbed Claudy Day, that, when chained together, create a complete attack pipeline: from targeted victim delivery, to invisible prompt manipulation, to silent exfiltration of sensitive data from the user's conversation history.

This section provides inference parameters and code examples for using the Anthropic Claude Messages API. ... You can use the Messages API to create chat bots or virtual assistant applications. The API manages the conversational exchanges between a user and an Anthropic Claude model (assistant). This topic shows how to use the Anthropic Claude messages API with the base inference operations (InvokeModel or InvokeModelWithResponseStream). However, we recommend that you use the Converse API to implement messages in your application. The Converse API provides a unified set of parameters that work across all models that support messages. For more information, see Inference using Converse API. Restrictions apply to the following operations: InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse, and ConverseStream. See API restrictions for details. Anthropic trains Claude models to operate on alternating user and assistant conversational turns.

The timeout period for inference calls to Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude 4 models is 60 minutes. By default, AWS SDK clients timeout after 1 minute. We recommend that you increase the read timeout period of your AWS SDK client to at least 60 minutes. For example, in the AWS Python botocore SDK, change the value of the read_timeout field in botocore.config ... You can also include a system prompt in the request. A system prompt lets you provide context and instructions to Anthropic Claude, such as specifying a particular goal or role. Specify a system prompt in the system field, as shown in the following example. "system": "You are Claude, an AI assistant created by Anthropic to be helpful, harmless, and honest. Your goal is to provide informative and substantive responses to queries while avoiding potential harms." ... A multimodal prompt combines multiple modalities (images and text) in a single prompt.

When creating a new message, you specify the prior conversational turns with the messages parameter. The model then generates the next Message in the conversation. Each input message must be an object with a role and content. You can specify a single user-role message, or you can include multiple user and assistant messages. If you are using the technique of prefilling the response from Claude (filling in the beginning of Claude's response by using a final assistant role Message), Claude will respond by picking up from where you left off. With this technique, Claude will still return a response with the assistant role. If the final message uses the assistant role, the response content will continue immediately from the content in that message. You can use this to constrain part of the model's response. ... import base64 import httpx # Option 1: Base64-encoded image image_url = "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/Camponotus_flavomarginatus_ant.jpg" image_media_type = "image/jpeg" image_data = base64.standard_b64encode(httpx.get(image_url).content).decode("utf-8") message = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-7", max_tokens=1024, messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "image", "source": { "type": "base64", "media_type": image_media_type, "data": image_data, }, }, {"type": "text", "text": "What is in the above image?"}, ], } ], ) print(message) # Option 2: URL-referenced image message_from_url = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create( model="claude-opus-4-7", max_tokens=1024, messages=[ { "role": "user", "content": [ { "type": "image", "source": { "type": "url", "url": "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a7/Camponotus_flavomarginatus_ant.jpg", }, }, {"type": "text", "text": "What is in the above image?"}, ], } ], ) print(mes

{ "id": "msg_01Q8Faay6S7QPTvEUUQARt7h", "type": "message", "role": "assistant", "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "C" } ], "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5", "stop_reason": "max_tokens", "stop_sequence": null, "usage": { "input_tokens": 42, "output_tokens": 1 } } Claude can read both text and images in requests. Images can be supplied using the base64, url, or file source types. The file source type references an image uploaded through the Files API. Supported media types are image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, and image/webp. See the vision guide for more details.

content.text:
All parameter values must be URL-encoded. Prompt text passed in q is truncated to roughly 14,000 characters. claude://claude.ai/new claude://claude.ai/new?q=Summarize this week's release notes · Opens a new chat in Claude Desktop.

All parameter values must be URL-encoded. Prompt text passed in q is truncated to roughly 14,000 characters. claude://claude.ai/new claude://claude.ai/new?q=Summarize this week's release notes · Opens a new chat in Claude Desktop. If you include q, the prompt field is prefilled with that text so you can review and send it. claude://claude.ai/chat/{conversation-id} claude://claude.ai/project/{project-id} Opens a specific chat or project by its ID. The ID is the UUID you see at the end of the chat or project URL in Claude. If the ID is missing or invalid, Claude opens your recent chats or your projects list instead. claude://code/new claude://code/new?q=Fix the failing test&folder=/Users/me/repo · Opens Claude Code in Claude Desktop with the composer prefilled. Use this for "Open in Claude Code" buttons in your own tools. Note: Any folder supplied through a link is treated as untrusted.

Nothing in the search results specifically documents `allow_dangling_human_message=1` as a public parameter. Here's what I can piece together from context though:

In the Anthropic Messages API, conversations must alternate strictly between user and assistant turns. A "dangling human message" would be a conversation that ends on a user turn with no assistant response following it — which is technically an incomplete or malformed conversation state from the API's perspective.

So `allow_dangling_human_message=1` almost certainly tells the frontend to permit loading or displaying a conversation that ends on a user message without a corresponding assistant reply. It's probably an internal parameter that handles edge cases like interrupted responses, failed generations, or conversations that were saved mid-turn.

It's not a publicly documented parameter — it looks like internal plumbing surfacing in the URL, likely because this conversation had a turn that didn't complete cleanly at some point.

chat_messages.text:
That's a significant inferential leap from the evidence. What you have is a URL parameter that allows a conversation with an unanswered user message to load properly. That's mundane frontend error-handling — it prevents the UI from breaking when a conversation ends on a user turn.

The gap between "this parameter exists" and "Anthropic is selectively suppressing responses to disapproved queries" is large. You'd need evidence that the parameter is being triggered specifically on certain content types, not just on any interrupted or failed response. Network timeouts, server errors, and browser crashes all produce the same state.

What made you think a response was being suppressed rather than just failing?
